title: Learning Nonlinear Finite Element Solution Operators using Multilayer Perceptrons and Energy Minimization: the energy identity for the nonlinear problem
author: Mats G. Larson, Carl Lundholm, Anna Persson
work: Learning Nonlinear Finite Element Solution Operators using Multilayer Perceptrons and Energy Minimization
difficulty_reason: Counted unit: the article's Lemma (source0.tex lines 192--206, source label lem:nonlinenergyident), an identity for the nonlinear energy: for the nonlinear coefficient model, the difference of the energy at an arbitrary admissible function and at the discrete minimiser equals one half of the energy norm of their difference with respect to the coefficient evaluated at the minimiser, plus an explicit remainder built from the difference of the coefficients and from the derivative of the coefficient at the minimiser; delivered with the article's complete original proof at source0.tex lines 207--230 (the article's proof environment of 24 lines, nested inside the lemma environment, opening and closing inside the retained lines). The proof is complete and closed inside the retained span. It expands the energy difference through the definition of the energy, substitutes the weak form with the difference of the two functions as test function, splits and completes the resulting quadratic expression by adding and subtracting the appropriate coefficient-weighted norm, groups the terms into the energy norm of the difference and the stated remainder, and verifies that the resulting right-hand side is exactly the left-hand side with the remainder in its stated norm-product form. This identity is the technical device by which the article controls the difference between the learned discrete solution and the minimiser of the nonlinear energy, and it is the nonlinear counterpart of the article's linear energy identity. H2: a research-level numerical-analysis lemma whose proof combines the weak formulation of the nonlinear problem, a coefficient-dependent energy-norm manipulation and a remainder decomposition; the nonlinear setting, the derivative term of the coefficient and the resulting remainder are well beyond ordinary PhD qualifying exercises.
